slides.title: Network architectures: client-server vs peer-to-peer
slides.body:
**Client-server**:
- Authoritative server runs game simulation.
- Clients send INPUTS to server; receive game state from server.
- Server resolves all gameplay (collision, damage, spawning).
- Pros: cheat-resistant; consistent state for all players.
- Cons: latency hurts (round-trip to server); server hosting cost; geographic disadvantage for distant players.
- Used by: most modern multiplayer (Fortnite, CS, Valorant, Overwatch).

**Peer-to-peer (P2P)**:
- Each player runs simulation; broadcast inputs to all others.
- Lockstep: all peers execute same simulation, advance together.
- Pros: low cost (no server); near-LAN latency on good networks.
- Cons: trust everyone; one cheating peer corrupts all. Vulnerable to NAT issues. Doesn't scale beyond ~8 players.
- Used by: RTS games (StarCraft, AoE), some fighting games, peer-to-peer co-op.

**Hybrid (relay-server)**:
- Server routes packets between peers (no game logic on server).
- Better NAT + bandwidth handling.
- Examples: Steam relay, AWS GameLift Relay.

**Latency**:
- LAN: 1-5 ms.
- Same-continent server: 30-80 ms.
- Trans-continental: 100-200 ms.
- Mobile / satellite: 100-1000 ms.

Games need to hide latency. Fast-paced FPS / fighting needs <100 ms 'feels responsive'. RTS / turn-based: 200-500 ms acceptable.

**Bandwidth**: tens of KB/s per player typical. Don't send full game state; send DELTAS (just what changed) + use prediction (next slide). Quake (1996) pioneered delta-compression at ~5 KB/s per player.

slides.title: Lockstep + rollback netcode
slides.body:
**Lockstep**: all peers run identical simulation, advance together. Inputs are exchanged each frame.
```
for each frame f:
  collect own input
  send input(f) to all peers
  wait for inputs from all peers for frame f
  advance simulation by 1 step using all inputs
```

Works if simulation is DETERMINISTIC: same inputs → same state on every machine. Requires fixed timestep + reproducible math (no float drift). RTS games (StarCraft, AoE) use this. Bandwidth low: just inputs.

Problem: must WAIT for the slowest peer's input. 200 ms ping → 5 frames of input lag (at 25 Hz). Input lag is THE fighting-game enemy.

**Rollback netcode** (GGPO, modern fighting games):
1. Send your own input immediately.
2. PREDICT the opponent's input (e.g., 'same as last frame' or 'idle').
3. Run simulation forward using predictions.
4. When real opponent input arrives (delayed): ROLLBACK to that frame; replay with real input + your own; arrive at corrected state.

Result: you feel responsive (no input delay on your actions); rollbacks invisible if prediction was correct or correction is small.

**Requirements**:
- Deterministic simulation (same inputs → same state).
- Fast save/restore (save state every frame to roll back to).
- Robust to small corrections (animation snapping is jarring).

**Used in**: Street Fighter 6, Tekken 8, Skullgirls, Killer Instinct, Mortal Kombat 11, Guilty Gear Strive. Has revolutionized online fighting games (previously dominated by delay-based netcode which felt sluggish).

**Frame data**: fighting games operate at 60 Hz with FRAME-PERFECT input requirements. Rollback netcode preserves frame accuracy. Massively reduces 'this game is unplayable online' complaints.

**Open-source**: GGPO (now relaunched as 'rollback') is open-source rollback library; many indie fighting games use it.

slides.title: Latency hiding: prediction + interpolation
slides.body:
**Client-side prediction**: don't wait for server response to move your character. Apply movement locally immediately. When server confirms, reconcile.
```
player presses 'W':
  immediately move forward locally
  send 'pressed W at time T' to server
  server processes, sends back authoritative position
  if local position matches server: nothing to do
  if doesn't match: snap to server (or smoothly correct)
```
Result: input feels responsive. Mispredictions cause occasional snaps (mostly visible when colliding with new players or obstacles).

**Entity interpolation**: for OTHER players (remote entities), DON'T predict their movement. Instead:
1. Buffer their position updates (rendered with ~100 ms delay).
2. Interpolate between buffered positions for smooth motion.
3. Renders 'old' but smooth.

Why: predicting other players' actions is unreliable; you'd need to redraw on every correction (jarring). Better to delay them slightly + show smooth interpolated motion.

**Lag compensation** (Valve's Counter-Strike model 1999+):
- Server REMEMBERS each player's position for the last N ms.
- When a player shoots, server rewinds OTHER players to their position at the shoot time (as the shooter saw them).
- Hit detection runs in this rewound state.
- Result: 'shoot what you see' (no leading needed).

**Trade-off**: a player with 200 ms ping can shoot 'around corners' from the perspective of a low-ping player. Compromise the game has long accepted.

**Snapshot interpolation** (Quake / Source engine):
- Server sends snapshots ~20 times per second.
- Clients interpolate between snapshots for rendering.
- Combine with prediction for own player.

**Tickrate**: server's simulation frequency. Higher = less latency + more bandwidth + more CPU. CS:GO 64-tick (default) vs 128-tick (premium servers). 60 tick standard for many games.

**Hit registration**: 'Why didn't my shot count?' Common complaint. Caused by combination of: ping, lag compensation limits, hit-box vs visual mismatch, server reconciliation. Tools (Spectate cam, kill cam) help diagnose.

question.question: Apply client-side prediction
question.goal: Player has 100 ms round-trip ping. Server runs at 60 Hz (16.7 ms per tick). Player presses 'fire' at local time T.

steps.prompt: Without prediction, the player sees nothing happen until server response arrives. After how long?
steps.reveal: 100 ms delay between press + visible effect. Feels sluggish.

steps.prompt: With client-side prediction: player sees firing animation immediately (locally). Meanwhile send 'fire at T' to server. Server processes at ~T+50 ms (one-way trip), confirms or corrects. Net effect on perceived input latency?

options: Essentially 0 (immediate local response). Server confirms within 100 ms; if confirmed, no correction needed. If shot didn't actually hit (server says miss), correction snap.

steps.reveal: Effectively 0 latency for input feedback. Server confirms within 100 ms; if disagreement, local state snaps. Most actions don't have disagreements. Used universally in modern multiplayer.

steps.prompt: Sometimes prediction is wrong (player thought they hit, server says no). How is the correction shown?

options: Smoothly interpolate to server's state over a few frames, or just accept the snap (small enough to be unnoticeable). Hit-effect cleanup (remove faked impact). For fast-paced games, snapping is acceptable as long as it's rare.

steps.reveal: Smooth correction over 100-300 ms or snap if difference is small (<10 cm). Hit-effects cleaned up if predicted hit was wrong. 'Lag spike' visible as the snap; players have learned to recognize it.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Prediction + lag compensation: hide network latency from player}}$$ Modern multiplayer is built on these techniques. Quake (1996) pioneered prediction; Counter-Strike formalized lag compensation; League of Legends + Overwatch + Fortnite all use refined versions. Without prediction, online games would feel as bad as they did in the dial-up era. Players have come to expect responsive controls regardless of ping.

question.question: Why do modern fighting games (Street Fighter 6, Tekken 8) use ROLLBACK netcode instead of traditional delay-based?
options: Rollback preserves frame-accurate input responsiveness regardless of opponent's ping; delay-based makes inputs sluggish (waits for all peers). Fighting games are frame-perfect by design — rollback is the only viable netcode for the competitive scene.
question.explanation: Fighting games operate at 60 Hz with frame-perfect input timing (a 1-frame parry, a 3-frame jab). Delay-based netcode forces the WHOLE simulation to wait for the slowest peer's input — adding input lag for everyone. 200 ms ping = 12 frames of lag = game becomes unplayable competitively. Rollback runs your inputs immediately, predicts opponent, rolls back when corrected. Massively superior UX. Tekken 7 stayed delay-based for years + the community complained; SF6 + Tekken 8 went rollback + the online scene revitalized.

slides.workedSolution: Delay-based: all peers wait for slowest, ~ping-of-frames of input lag for everyone. Rollback: your inputs are instant; opponent inputs predicted + rolled-back if wrong. Player feels responsive even at 100 ms ping. Hard: requires deterministic sim + fast save/restore. GGPO library + modern engine support made it tractable. Now industry standard for fighting games.

Choosing netcode for a co-op game
question.prompt: A team builds a 4-player co-op survival game. Walk through the netcode architecture decision (client-server, P2P, lockstep, prediction).
Explain in two or three sentences why client-side prediction is essential for any responsive multiplayer game beyond LAN-only.
question.rubric: Mentions that any network ping >50 ms makes inputs feel sluggish without prediction; prediction lets the player see immediate response to inputs (locally) while the server confirms; lag compensation lets the server reconcile despite ping differences; without these techniques, online games are unplayable at typical internet latencies.
